craft_claim: Fanciful invention reads as delight rather than error only when the voice keeps a legible play frame, signalling that the invented thing is an invitation to imagine and not a claim about the world.

supporting_evidence.location: Steps to an Ecology of Mind (1972), pp. 177-193; orig. Psychiatric Research Reports 2:39-51 (1955)
supporting_evidence.note: Bateson argues play depends on metacommunicative signals carrying the message 'this is play'; the playful nip denotes the bite but does not denote what the bite denotes, so the frame brackets real consequence and holds two levels at once.

supporting_evidence.location: 1926 collection, narrative voice across the stories
supporting_evidence.note: Milne's narrator addresses the child reader as a co-player, framing each episode as a story being told inside a small, safe world; the frame lets the reader enjoy impossible events without treating them as falsehoods.

counterevidence.note: The frame is not the only route to aesthetic delight: Abhinavagupta's camatkara describes an absorbed, commonized wonder that is not framed as pretense, so 'play frame' should be treated as one mechanism among several in the card.

scope: Narrative, essay, and marketing prose that invites a fanciful rather than literal reading.
exceptions: Texts that deliberately break the frame to shock (metafictional reversals) belong to satire or horror, not this tone.
Devotional or mythic wonder may use invention without a play frame; that is closer to tone-reverent.
